2.3.1:
Why this matters

Every decision in Six Sigma rests on data, and data comes from measurement. If the measurement itself is wrong or noisy, the team will chase variation that is not really there, or miss real problems. Measurement System Analysis (MSA) checks the measuring before you trust the measurements. It is a required Measure-phase deliverable.

The big idea

A measurement system is everything involved in getting a number: the instrument (gauge, scale, software), the people using it, the method, the environment and the part being measured. Like any process, it has variation.

What you see in your data is a mix of two things:

σ²(observed) = σ²(process) + σ²(measurement)

The variation you observe is the real process variation plus the measurement system's own variation. (Variances add, as in 2.2.2.) If the measurement variation is large, it hides the real process.

Example: observed σ = 5 minutes, measurement system σ = 3 minutes. Real process σ = √(5² − 3²) = √16 = 4 minutes. A quarter of what looked like process variation was really measurement noise.

Accuracy vs precision

Picture shooting at a target:

Accuracy is about where the shots center; precision is about how tightly they group.

  • Accuracy: how close the average of measurements is to the true value. An accurate scale, on average, reads the true weight.
  • Precision: how close repeated measurements are to each other. A precise scale gives nearly the same reading every time you weigh the same thing, even if that reading is wrong.

A measurement can be precise but not accurate (tight group, wrong place), which is usually easy to fix by calibration. It can be accurate but not precise (centered but scattered), which is harder: the instrument or method itself is noisy.

The five measurement errors

MSA breaks measurement error into two families:

Location errors (accuracy problems): is the average reading in the right place?

  1. Bias: the average reading differs from the true value.
  2. Linearity: bias changes across the range of sizes being measured.
  3. Stability: bias changes over time (drift).

Spread errors (precision problems): are the readings consistent?

  1. Repeatability: variation when the same person measures the same part with the same instrument several times. Also called equipment variation.
  2. Reproducibility: variation between different people measuring the same parts. Also called appraiser variation.

2.3.2 covers location errors; 2.3.3 covers repeatability and reproducibility.

Resolution (discrimination)

Resolution (or discrimination) is the smallest change the instrument can show. A scale that reads only to the nearest 100 lb cannot tell a 40,020 lb load from a 40,080 lb load.

Rule of thumb: the measurement increments should be no bigger than about one-tenth of the tolerance (specification width), or of the process spread. If the tolerance is ±1.0 mm (width 2.0 mm), the gauge should read to 0.2 mm or finer, ideally 0.1 mm. With too coarse a resolution, many different parts get the same reading and the data looks blocky.

Calibration

Calibration compares an instrument against a reference standard of known value (traceable to national standards) and adjusts it if needed. Calibration fixes bias at the points checked. It does not fix poor repeatability or reproducibility. A calibrated gauge can still be imprecise.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Precise but not accurate: a tight cluster far from the center.
  • Observed variation = process + measurement, as variances.
  • Calibration fixes bias, not precision.
  • Resolution: about 1/10 of tolerance or process spread, or finer.

Check yourself

  1. Define accuracy and precision in one sentence each.
  2. A gauge always reads 0.5 kg high, very consistently. Is it accurate? Precise?
  3. Observed σ is 10 and measurement σ is 6. What is the real process σ?
  4. Which errors are "location" errors?
  5. The tolerance is 0.50 mm wide. What resolution should the gauge have, at least?
Show answers
  1. Accuracy: how close the average reading is to the true value. Precision: how close repeated readings are to each other.
  2. Precise but not accurate (it has bias).
  3. √(100 − 36) = √64 = 8.
  4. Bias, linearity, stability.
  5. About 0.05 mm or finer.

Key takeaways

  • Observed variance = process variance + measurement variance.
  • Accuracy = centered on truth; precision = consistent.
  • Location errors: bias, linearity, stability. Spread errors: repeatability, reproducibility.
  • Resolution about one-tenth of the tolerance or process spread.
  • Calibration fixes bias only.
2.3.2:
Why this matters

A gauge that reads wrong in a consistent way can make a good process look bad, or a bad one look good. These three studies find and describe location errors so they can be corrected.

Bias

Bias is the difference between the average of repeated measurements and the true (reference) value:

Bias = average measured value − reference value

How to study it: take a reference part whose true value is known (measured by a more accurate lab method, or a certified standard). Measure it many times (often 10 or more) with the gauge under normal conditions. Average the readings.

Example: a reference weight of 10.00 kg is weighed 10 times; the average is 10.03 kg. Bias = 10.03 − 10.00 = +0.03 kg: the scale reads high by 0.03 kg on average.

Whether that bias matters depends on how it compares with the tolerance and with the variation of the readings (a statistical test can show whether the bias is significantly different from zero). Fix: calibrate or adjust the gauge.

Linearity

Linearity describes how bias changes across the operating range of the gauge. A gauge might be accurate for small parts but read high for large ones.

If bias stayed flat at zero across all sizes, the gauge would have no linearity problem.

How to study it: measure several reference parts that span the range the gauge is used for (small to large), several times each. Plot bias against reference value and fit a line. A flat line at zero means no linearity problem. A sloped line means bias depends on size.

Fixes: a linearity problem is usually not solved by a single calibration offset. Options include calibrating at several points, repairing worn components, or using a different gauge or method for part of the range.

Stability

Stability (also called drift) describes how bias changes over time. A scale might read correctly on Monday and drift high by Friday as it warms up or wears.

How to study it: measure the same master part periodically (for example daily) over weeks, and plot the results on a control chart (5.2). A stable gauge shows only random scatter around a steady center. Shifts, trends or out-of-control points show instability.

Fixes depend on the cause: environment (temperature, vibration), wear, maintenance schedule, warm-up time, or a need for more frequent calibration.

Telling them apart

DescriptionError
"Reads consistently 2 units high"Bias
"Reads correctly on small parts, high on large parts"Linearity
"Was fine last month, reads higher every week"Stability

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Bias = average − reference, not a single reading.
  • Linearity is across sizes; stability is across time.
  • Stability is tracked with a control chart on a master part.
  • One calibration offset fixes bias, not linearity.

Check yourself

  1. A reference part is 50.0 mm. Readings average 49.8 mm. What is the bias?
  2. A thermometer is accurate at 20 °C but reads 3 degrees low at 80 °C. Which error?
  3. How would you monitor a gauge's stability?
  4. What does a flat line at zero on a linearity plot mean?
  5. Which of the three is usually fixed by a simple calibration?
Show answers
  1. 49.8 − 50.0 = −0.2 mm (reads low).
  2. Linearity.
  3. Measure the same master part regularly over time and plot it on a control chart.
  4. No linearity problem: bias is zero across the whole range.
  5. Bias.

Key takeaways

  • Bias = average measured − reference; fix with calibration.
  • Linearity = bias changing across the measurement range; check with several reference parts.
  • Stability = bias changing over time; track a master part on a control chart.
2.3.3:
Why this matters

Gage R&R is the most important MSA study. It answers: how much of the variation in our data is caused by the measurement system itself? If the answer is "a lot", no analysis built on that data can be trusted, and the gauge or method must be fixed first.

The big idea

Total observed variation splits into pieces:

  • Part-to-part variation: the real differences between parts. This is what we want to see.
  • Measurement system variation (GRR): noise added by measuring. It has two parts:
  • Repeatability (equipment variation, EV): the same person measuring the same part repeatedly with the same gauge gets different readings.
  • Reproducibility (appraiser variation, AV): different people measuring the same parts get different averages.

Because independent variances add:

GRR = √(repeatability² + reproducibility²)
Total variation = √(GRR² + part-to-part²)

(each term here is a standard deviation).

Running a study

A typical (not mandatory) design:

  • About 10 parts that span the full range of the process, so the study can see real part differences.
  • 2 or 3 operators (appraisers) who normally do the measuring.
  • 2 or 3 repeat measurements per operator per part.
  • Randomized order and blind measuring: operators should not know which part they are measuring or what they measured last time, otherwise they unconsciously repeat their earlier readings.

This is a crossed study: every operator measures every part. When measuring destroys the part (a crash test, a tensile test), each operator must measure different but similar parts, which is a nested study.

Analysis methods: the ANOVA method (preferred; it can also detect an operator-by-part interaction) and the older Xbar-R method (simpler, using ranges).

The key metrics

%Study Variation (%SV, also %GRR): the measurement system's share of the total variation, on a standard deviation basis.

%Study Var = GRR ÷ Total variation × 100

%Tolerance: the measurement system's spread compared with the specification width.

%Tolerance = (6 × GRR) ÷ (USL − LSL) × 100

The "6" is the study spread: 6σ covers about 99.73% of measurements. Older material used 5.15σ (99%); check which a question uses.

%Contribution: the same comparison using variances instead of standard deviations:

%Contribution = GRR² ÷ Total variation² × 100

Because it is a squared ratio, %Contribution numbers are much smaller: a 10% Study Var is about a 1% Contribution, and 30% Study Var is about 9% Contribution.

Number of distinct categories (ndc): how many groups of parts the measurement system can reliably tell apart.

ndc = 1.41 × (part-to-part σ ÷ GRR)

ndc should be at least 5. It is truncated to a whole number (5.9 counts as 5), not rounded up.

Acceptance criteria

The AIAG guidelines (as used by Minitab):

%Study Var (or %Tolerance)Verdict
Under 10%Acceptable
10% to 30%May be acceptable, depending on the importance of the measurement, the cost of the gauge and the cost of fixing it
Over 30%Unacceptable: improve the measurement system

Equivalent %Contribution cutoffs are about 1% and 9%.

Which percentage to use? %Tolerance is the better guide when the gauge is used to sort parts as good or bad against specifications. %Study Var is the better guide when the data will be used to study and improve the process (seeing process variation). A gauge can look fine on one and poor on the other.

Reading the results: what is causing the noise?

  • Repeatability much larger than reproducibility: the problem is the equipment or method. The gauge needs maintenance, a better fixture, a more stable setup, or replacement.
  • Reproducibility much larger than repeatability: the problem is how different people measure. Fix with training, clearer operational definitions, standard technique, or a fixture that removes judgment.
  • Significant operator × part interaction (from ANOVA): some operators measure certain parts differently (for example, one operator struggles with very small parts). Investigate technique on those parts.

Gage R&R software also shows graphs:

  • R chart by operator: shows repeatability; points should be in control (operators are consistent).
  • Xbar chart by operator: should show many points outside the limits, because the limits come from measurement noise and the parts should differ by much more. If most points are inside the limits, the gauge cannot tell the parts apart.

Worked example

A study on a tire tread gauge gives (as standard deviations, in mm):

  • Repeatability = 0.03
  • Reproducibility = 0.04
  • Part-to-part = 0.24
  • Tolerance (USL − LSL) = 2.0 mm
  1. GRR = √(0.03² + 0.04²) = √(0.0009 + 0.0016) = √0.0025 = 0.05.
  2. Total = √(0.05² + 0.24²) = √(0.0025 + 0.0576) = √0.0601 ≈ 0.245.
  3. %Study Var = 0.05 ÷ 0.245 × 100 ≈ 20.4%: marginal (10% to 30%).
  4. %Tolerance = 6 × 0.05 ÷ 2.0 × 100 = 15%: marginal.
  5. %Contribution = 0.0025 ÷ 0.0601 ≈ 4.2%.
  6. ndc = 1.41 × 0.24 ÷ 0.05 = 6.77, truncated to 6: acceptable (at least 5).
  7. Reproducibility (0.04) is larger than repeatability (0.03), so operator technique is the bigger issue. Training and a standard method would be the first fix.

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Add variances, not standard deviations, to combine repeatability and reproducibility.
  • %Contribution is on a variance basis; do not compare its numbers with the 10%/30% cutoffs.
  • ndc truncates; 4.9 is 4, which fails.
  • Repeatability = equipment; reproducibility = operators.
  • Parts should span the process range; if the parts are too similar, part-to-part variation looks small and the gauge looks worse than it is.
  • 6σ vs 5.15σ study spread.

Check yourself

  1. Define repeatability and reproducibility.
  2. Repeatability σ = 0.6, reproducibility σ = 0.8. What is GRR?
  3. GRR = 1.0 and total variation = 4.0. What is %Study Var, and is it acceptable?
  4. GRR = 0.5, tolerance = 12. What is %Tolerance (6σ basis)?
  5. Part σ = 3.2 and GRR = 1.0. What is ndc, and is it acceptable?
  6. Reproducibility is the dominant source. What do you fix?
Show answers
  1. Repeatability: variation when one operator measures the same part repeatedly with the same gauge. Reproducibility: variation between different operators measuring the same parts.
  2. √(0.36 + 0.64) = √1 = 1.0.
  3. 1.0 ÷ 4.0 = 25%: may be acceptable depending on the application.
  4. 6 × 0.5 ÷ 12 = 25%.
  5. 1.41 × 3.2 ÷ 1.0 = 4.51, truncated to 4: not acceptable (needs at least 5).
  6. Operator technique: training, clear operational definitions, standard method or fixtures.

Key takeaways

  • GRR = √(repeatability² + reproducibility²); total = √(GRR² + part²).
  • %Study Var = GRR ÷ total; %Tolerance = 6 × GRR ÷ (USL − LSL); %Contribution uses variances.
  • Under 10% good, 10% to 30% maybe, over 30% unacceptable.
  • ndc = 1.41 × part σ ÷ GRR, truncated, at least 5.
  • Repeatability points to equipment; reproducibility points to operators.
2.3.4:
Why this matters

Not every measurement produces a number. Many inspections end in a judgment: pass or fail, damaged or not, good, minor defect or major defect. Those judgments need checking too, and they are often less reliable than people assume.

Variable vs attribute MSA

  • Variable MSA: the measurement is continuous (length, weight, time). Use Gage R&R (2.3.3) plus bias, linearity and stability.
  • Attribute MSA: the measurement is a category (pass/fail, good/bad, defect type). Use attribute agreement analysis.

Attribute agreement analysis

A typical design:

  • 30 to 50 items, chosen to include a good mix of good and bad, and some borderline cases, with the correct answer (the standard or reference) known for each, decided by an expert.
  • 2 or 3 appraisers (inspectors).
  • Each appraiser judges each item 2 or 3 times, in random order, without knowing which item it is.

The analysis checks four kinds of agreement:

  1. Within appraiser: does each inspector agree with themselves across repeated trials? (like repeatability)
  2. Between appraisers: do the inspectors agree with each other? (like reproducibility)
  3. Each appraiser vs standard: is each inspector right? (accuracy)
  4. All appraisers vs standard: do all inspectors, on all trials, match the correct answer?

Agreement is not accuracy. Three inspectors can agree perfectly with each other and all be wrong, for example if they were all trained on the same incorrect standard. Always check agreement against the known standard.

Percent agreement and kappa

The simplest measure is percent agreement: the share of items rated the same way. But some agreement happens by chance: if two inspectors pass 90% of items at random, they would agree most of the time without really looking. Kappa (κ) corrects for chance:

κ = (Pₒ − Pₑ) ÷ (1 − Pₑ)
  • Pₒ: the observed proportion of agreement.
  • Pₑ: the proportion of agreement expected by chance alone.
  • κ = 1: perfect agreement. κ = 0: no better than chance. κ below 0: worse than chance.

Worked example. Two inspectors judge 50 trailers as "damaged" or "OK". They agree on 45 (Pₒ = 0.90). Inspector A called 30 "OK" (60%) and B called 32 "OK" (64%).

  1. Chance agreement on "OK": 0.60 × 0.64 = 0.384.
  2. Chance agreement on "damaged": 0.40 × 0.36 = 0.144.
  3. Pₑ = 0.384 + 0.144 = 0.528.
  4. κ = (0.90 − 0.528) ÷ (1 − 0.528) = 0.372 ÷ 0.472 ≈ 0.79.

The 90% raw agreement shrinks to 0.79 once chance is removed.

How good is good enough?

Sources differ, so read the question for clues:

  • AIAG MSA manual: κ above 0.75 indicates good to excellent agreement; below 0.40 indicates poor agreement.
  • Some software rules of thumb (for example SigmaXL): 0.9 or above good, 0.7 to 0.9 marginal or acceptable, below 0.7 unacceptable.

By the AIAG rule the example's 0.79 is good. By the stricter rule it is marginal. It is not known which convention IASSC uses; when a question gives thresholds, use them.

Misclassification rates

When comparing with the standard, three rates describe the kinds of mistakes:

  • Effectiveness: the share of items classified correctly.
  • Miss rate: the share of bad items called good (defects escape to the customer). Usually the most serious error.
  • False alarm rate: the share of good items called bad (unnecessary rework, scrap or rejections).

The AIAG MSA manual gives example guidelines for each appraiser:

AcceptableMarginal (may need improvement)Unacceptable
Effectiveness90% or more80% or moreBelow 80%
Miss rate2% or less5% or lessAbove 5%
False alarm rate5% or less10% or lessAbove 10%

Other agreement statistics (recognition only)

  • Cohen's kappa: agreement between two raters (or one rater and the standard).
  • Fleiss' kappa: agreement among three or more raters.
  • Kendall's coefficient: for ordinal ratings (like severity 1 to 5), where some disagreements are bigger than others; it gives credit for being "close".

Common mistakes and exam traps

  • Kappa removes chance agreement; raw percent agreement overstates reliability.
  • Agreement with each other is not correctness: check against the standard.
  • AIAG: κ ≥ 0.75 good, < 0.40 poor. Some texts use 0.9 / 0.7.
  • Miss rate = bad passed as good; false alarm = good rejected as bad.
  • Include borderline items: an easy sample makes every inspector look perfect.

Check yourself

  1. When do you use attribute agreement analysis instead of Gage R&R?
  2. Pₒ = 0.85, Pₑ = 0.50. Calculate kappa.
  3. By the AIAG guideline, is κ = 0.62 good, poor, or in between?
  4. All three inspectors agree with each other on every item. Is the inspection system acceptable?
  5. An inspector passes 4 out of 50 damaged items. Which rate is affected?
Show answers
  1. When the measurement is categorical (pass/fail, defect type) rather than continuous.
  2. (0.85 − 0.50) ÷ (1 − 0.50) = 0.35 ÷ 0.50 = 0.70.
  3. In between (above 0.40, below 0.75).
  4. Not necessarily. They must also agree with the known standard; they could all be wrong together.
  5. The miss rate.

Key takeaways

  • Variable data: Gage R&R. Attribute data: attribute agreement analysis.
  • Check within appraiser, between appraisers, each vs standard, all vs standard.
  • κ = (Pₒ − Pₑ) ÷ (1 − Pₑ) removes chance agreement.
  • AIAG: κ above 0.75 good, below 0.40 poor; some software uses 0.9 and 0.7.
  • Effectiveness, miss rate and false alarm rate describe the kinds of errors.
